This value suggests a roughly 1,600-fold increase in body mass is required to reach the ultimate wet weight of 16,000,000 grams [Wwi = 16,000,000 grams], making this species one of the most extreme examples of postnatal somatic expansion among terrestrial reptiles. The trajectory from a 10-kilogram hatchling to a 16-metric-ton adult necessarily demands prolonged periods of intensive feeding and efficient assimilation. Field records indicate that juveniles exhibit a rapid growth phase during their first few decades, with the most pronounced mass gains coinciding with the onset of the warm season. The substantial gap between birth mass and asymptotic adult mass implies that reproductive investment per offspring is relatively low in proportional terms, though absolute energy expenditure per clutch is considerable when viewed through the lens of whole-organism metabolism. Mature individuals, confirmed through gonadal examination, often display subtle secondary sexual characteristics that correlate with body size, though sex-specific differences in ultimate mass are not yet well documented.

This value, however, is considered very speculative given the small sample size of gravid females studied and the difficulty of confirming true fecundity in a species with such protracted inter-breeding intervals. Each clutch typically contains several large, yolky eggs that require substantial maternal investment prior to oviposition. The annualized reproduction rate suggests that a single female could theoretically produce around 30 offspring under optimal thermal conditions, though actual recruitment in the wild is likely far lower due to high juvenile mortality and sporadic breeding opportunities. The challenges of documenting nesting events in remote floodplain habitats further contribute to the uncertainty surrounding these estimates. Comparative data from other large-bodied sauropsids indicate that such a low fecundity is consistent with a life-history strategy emphasizing high parental investment per offspring and extended developmental periods.

The lifespan of Camerasaurus has been estimated from mark-recapture studies and skeletal chronometry to reach approximately 100 years [am = approximately 100 years] when the animals maintain a core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This extraordinary longevity places the species among the longest-lived of all known reptiles, a feat likely facilitated by low extrinsic mortality rates in their predator-scarce adult environment and a slow pace of physiological aging. Isotopic analysis of growth rings in fossilized long bones corroborates the interpretation of a century-long life span, though captive individuals have yet to be observed beyond their eighth decade. The combination of a massive adult body size and a warm, stable thermal regime appears to be a key correlate of this extended survival. As body temperature is held at 37 °C, cellular repair mechanisms and metabolic efficiency may operate near an optimum that delays senescence. Understanding the interplay between thermoregulation and somatic maintenance in this species remains a priority for future comparative gerontology studies.

Such a slow maturation schedule imposes a demographic vulnerability, as populations experiencing elevated juvenile mortality may fail to replace themselves if recruitment is intermittent. Conservation managers have therefore emphasized the protection of sub-adult age classes to ensure long-term population viability.

First clutches are typically smaller than those produced by older, more experienced females, reflecting a gradual improvement in reproductive efficiency with age. Further studies tracking individually marked animals from the hatchling stage through their first nesting season will be essential to refine these preliminary estimates and to understand the ecological factors that modulate the timing of first breeding.
